list.listitem: Women with a family history of BRCA gene mutations and a positive screening should be referred for genetic counselling. They should be counselled on the risks, benefits, and limitations of genetic screening. B
Routine screening is not recommended with either CA-125 or ultrasound.A
The best initial study for women with suspected ovarian cancer is transvaginal ultrasound. C
Surgery is required with histopathologic evaluation for definitive diagnosis and staging. A
Chemotherapy for ovarian cancer should include a platinum-based drug, a taxane-based drug, and bevacizumab. PARP inhibitors as maintenance therapy increase progression free survival. A
Women with early disease at diagnosis and absence of residual tumor after treatment have better prognosis and improved survival. A
Ovarian cancer is the abnormal growth of cancer cells in one ovary, both ovaries, or the surface of the ovaries.
The overall age-adjusted incidence of is 11.7 cases per 100,000 for the years 2010 to 2014.
Age adjusted incidence rates differ across race and ethnicity.
White non-hispanic women tend to have higher rates than Blacks, Asians, American Indians, and Hispanics.
The age adjusted death rate is 7.4 per 100,000 women per year.
The approximate lifetime risk of developing cancer is 1.3 percent of women based on 2010 to 2014 data.
The prevalence of ovarian cancer in the United States is estimated at more than 222,060 women in 2014.
Eighty percent of women have nonlocalized disease at diagnosis. Women with localized disease have a higher 5-year survival rate.
Ovarian cancer commonly occurs in women between the ages of 55 to 64 with a median age of 63 according to SEER data.
The prevalence of ovarian tumors is 30 to 50 per 100,000 women with a lifetime risk of 1.4% for women who have no affected relatives.
Ovarian cancer is the seventh most common female cancer worldwide and the fifth most common cause of cancer death in US women.
Ovarian cancer is the second most common gynecologic cancer and has the highest mortality rate of all gynecologic cancers.

There are four major theories about the development of ovarian cancer: (1) "incessant ovulation"-repetitive ovulation resulting in traumatized epithelium leading to an estrogen-rich environment due to errors in DNA repair and a disrupted epithelial surface; (2) excessive gonadotropin secretion stimulating ovarian epithelial cells; (3) excessive androgen stimulation to ovarian epithelium leading to malignant transformation and (4) inflammation.

Family history is a major risk factor with increased risk for carriers of BRCA 1 and BRCA 2 gene mutations in those with a prior diagnosis of hereditary breast cancer. There is a decreased risk following prophylactic oophorectomy in women with BRCA gene mutations (NNT = 36 over 3.5 years).
KRAS variant is a risk factor for those women with a family history of breast and ovarian cancer.

TP53 mutations are found in high grade serous ovarian cancer. Other mutations occur and suggest a similar origin to breast cancer. NOTCH and FOXM1 signaling are found in the pathophysiology of serous ovarian cancer.

Increased number of pregnancies, oral contraceptive pill use (RR 0.52; 95% CI, 0.39-0.68), use of depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA), breastfeeding, and tubal ligation are associated with decreased risk. The odds ratio for ovarian cancer was 0.73 for ever users compared with never users of OCPs.

A systematic review of 29 retrospective studies found that overall cancer incidence was non-significantly higher in the fertility therapy group compared with women not receiving fertility therapy (OR 1.19; 95% CI, 0.98-1.46). Subgroup analyses, which should be interpreted cautiously due to unmeasured confounding and multiple comparisons, found a higher ovarian cancer incidence with fertility therapy for borderline ovarian tumors (OR 1.69; 95% CI, 1.03-1.69). It was also significantly higher in women receiving IVF (OR 1.32; 95% CI, 1.03-1.69) and clomiphene citrate (OR 1.40; 95% CI, 1.10-1.77).

A second umbrella meta-analysis of observational studies that compared the incidence of female-specific cancers among patients who underwent fertility treatments with the incidence among control patients in the general population identified positive associations for ovarian and borderline ovarian tumors. IVF as an infertility strategy had a significant association. However, evidence was relatively weak, and it is not clear that the original studies or meta-analyses accounted for differences in cancer risks due to infertility alone. The most we can conclude is that the fertility treatments, especially IVF, clomiphene, and human menopausal gonadotropin, might be associated with increased risk for ovarian cancer and borderline ovarian tumors. The authors found no associations with breast cancer.
Ovarian inclusion cysts are not associated with ovarian malignancy, based on early results from a large British RCT of ovarian cancer screening.
The risk of ovarian cancer is increased in persons with myotonic muscular dystrophy.
Ovarian cancer spreads locally to the peritoneum. Routes of metastases include hematogenous spread, lymphatic invasion, and transdiaphragmatic passage.
Eighty percent to 85% of malignant ovarian cancers are epithelial ovarian cancers.
Two thirds of ovarian neoplasms in younger women are dysgerminomas.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Family history in first- or second-degree relative
Two or 3 relatives with ovarian cancer
History of breast or colorectal cancer
Prophylactic oophorectomy in women with BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations
Increase BMI and history of hormone therapy

list.listitem: Women at risk for BRCA gene mutations should be referred for genetic counseling and possible BRCA screening. B
Screening for ovarian cancer in average-risk women with ultrasound, CA-125, or other tests is not recommended. A
Consider prophylactic oophorectomy for women with BRCA gene mutations (NNT = 36 over 3 years). B
The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends against routine screening for ovarian cancer (D recommendation) because of its low incidence and the lack of efficacy.

The PLCO trial randomized over 78,000 women age 55 to 74 years to annual CA-125 for 8 years and annual ultrasound for 4 years, or usual care. After a median of 12.8 years of follow-up, there was no significant difference in cancer specific mortality or all-cause mortality. One third of screened women with a false positive underwent surgery as a result, and 15% of them had a major treatment related adverse event.
The USPSTF recommends genetic counselling and BRCA testing for women who have a family history of hereditary breast and/or ovarian cancer (Grade B recommendation).

Initial results from the UK Collaborative Trial of Ovarian Cancer Screening (UKCTOCS) were published in December, 2015. At that point, women had been followed for 8 to 10 years, with only a quarter followed for 13 years. In this study, 100,000 women received usual care, 50,000 annual ultrasound, and 50,000 annual CA-125 interpreted using the "Risk of Ovarian Cancer Algorithm" (ROCA) that essentially identified a normal range for each women and triggered further investigation when that range was exceeded (even if lower than the traditional cutoff of 35 ng/ml). The primary analysis did not find a statistically significant ovarian cancer specific mortality benefit. Analyses using a different set of statistical assumptions, and analyses limited to only those women followed for 13 years, suggested a possible significant reduction in mortality. However this reduction is small (50 fewer deaths per 100,000 women) and will require at least 3 more years of follow-up of the entire population to confirm them.

Final results of the UKCTOCS were published in 2021 and found that after a median 16 years of follow-up, cancer specific mortality was 0.6% in each group: ROCA algorithm, ultrasound only, or no screening.

A systematic review found that the bimanual exam was approximately 44% sensitive, with a positive preditive value of only 1% when used in a screening population. It cannot be recommended as a screening test.

Women with a personal history of breast or colon cancer should receive genetic counselling and BRCA testing; women with a personal history of endometrial cancer should be considered for genetic counselling.

A nonrandomized population-based trial found a risk reduction in women with BRCA gene mutations undergoing bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for cancer of the ovary, fallopian tubes, and peritoneum (NNT = 36 over 3 years).
Oral contraceptives decrease the risk of developing ovarian cancer.
Ovarian cancer may present with nonspecific symptoms and continues to be a disease diagnosed in late stage.
Women with low risk ovarian cancer that have adequate staging are treated by surgery and have survival rates >90%.
The best initial study for women with suspected ovarian cancer is transvaginal ultrasound.
Surgery is required with histopathologic evaluation for definitive diagnosis and staging.

Differential.Differential_Features: Ascites, mobile septations, peritoneal, and omental thickenings on ultrasound
Differentiate by ultrasound appearance or histology following biopsy or excision
Fever, pain, cervical motion tenderness, cervical discharge
Meets Rome criteria, more prominent gastrointestinal symptoms

list.listitem: See for staging system for ovarian cancer.
A careful family history is the single most important factor in determining the likelihood of ovarian cancer (see risk factors).

Women with ovarian cancer can be asymptomatic or present with nonspecific findings, such as abdominal distension, pain, urinary symptoms, and gastrointestinal symptoms, including bloating, constipation, and abdominal pain. Patients with or more symptoms have a significant increase in the likelihood of ovarian cancer (LR+ >5.0). More than 50% of women present with irritable bowel-like symptoms.

The National Comprehensive Cancer Network recommends an abdominal and pelvic examination when ovarian cancer is suspected. Ovarian cancer identified on screening pelvic examination is usually advanced and use of the pelvic examination as a screening test is not recommended. A systematic review found that the bimanual exam was approximately 44% sensitive, with a positive preditive value of only 1% when used in a screening population. The most common finding on physical examination is abdominal distension, usually indicative of ascites.
Other nonspecific signs and symptoms are abnormal vaginal bleeding, pelvic pressure, pelvic pain, and back pain.

NICE guidelines recommend evaluation with ultrasound if CA-125 is 35 IU/ml or greater in women with persistent, frequent abdominal distension or bloating, early satiety or loss of appetite, pelvic or abdominal pain, or increased urinary urgency and/or frequency.

A systematic review found that the symptoms most increasing the likelihood of ovarian cancer when present were abdominal mass (LR+ 30), abdominal distension or increased girth (LR+ 16), abdominal or pelvic pain (LR+ 10), bloating (LR+ 9), loss of appetite (LR+ 9), and family history (LR+ 7).

Perform a pregnancy test prior to any imaging studies. The best initial imaging study for women with suspected ovarian cancer is transvaginal ultrasound. The transvaginal approach enhances detection of ovarian size, characteristics and texture, location, and site of tumor. Malignancy is suspected with a mass larger than 4 cm, thickened walls greater than 3 mm, papillary necrosis, nodularity, various degrees of solid components, and necrosis or hemorrhage.

The Ovarian-Adnexal Reporting and Data System (O-RADS) is recommended as a framework for assessing the likelihood of ovarian cancer in women with adnexal lesions. A study in 913 women found the likilihood of malignant neoplasm was 0.5% with O-RADS 2, 4.5% with O-RADS 3, 11.6% with O-RADS 4, and 66% with O-RADS 5.

Also order chest X-ray, CA-125, CBC, and liver function tests as a part of the initial evaluation, and consider gastrointestinal evaluation. Definitive diagnosis and staging requires laparotomy or laparoscopy followed by histopathologic tissue evaluation.

Color flow Doppler can be used to evaluate blood flow within the ovaries. Malignant tumors have increased neovascularity. If the transvaginal ultrasound is indeterminate or suspicious for malignancy, a CA-125 is obtained and surgical exploration is performed with laparoscopy (if CA-125 result is normal) or laparotomy (if CA-125 result is abnormal and/or there is suspected omental involvement, ascites, pleural effusion, or other systemic symptoms).
CA-125 most useful in monitoring ovarian cancer after chemotherapy; alone, it is not an accurate diagnostic test.
CT is the preferred imaging study when assessing patients for metastatic disease or recurrence.
The ADNEX risk prediction model to distinguish pre-operatively between benign, borderline and malignant ovarian disease has been validated in over 2000 women and appears to be an effective model.

Ovarian inclusion cysts are often an incidental finding. A large cohort study of over 50,000 women found that there was no difference in the risk of ovarian cancer after 6 years in women with an inclusion cyst compared to those without a cyst.

A 2021 guideline from the Society of Obstetrics and Gynaecology of Canada recommends that evaluation of the woman with an adnexal mass begin with a careful history and physical examination including lymph node examination, lung exam for pleural effusion or consolidation, breast and axillary examination for breast mass, and abdominal exam for ascites, omental caking, and organomegaly. The pelvic exam should include both bimanual and rectovaginal exam.

Initial imaging should be with ultrasound. If there is a solid component with a strong/central color flow, 4 or more papillary projects >3 mm in height, thick multiple irregular septations, or ascites and peritoneal nodulariry, these women should receive immediate referral to a gynecologic oncologist. If referral is delayed, order tumor markers and CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis.
If the ultrasound is indeterminate, obtain MRI or refer to a gynecologic oncologist.
The guideline recommends that for women less than 40 years of age, rare forms of ovarian cancer be considered and that HCG, LDH and alpha-fetoprotein should be obtained.
For women with bilateral masses that appear malignant on ultrasound, refer to a gynecologic oncologist and also order CEA, CA 19-9, and CA 15-3 tumor markers.
See for guidance regarding evaluation for possible ovarian malignancy in a pregnant person.

A Cochrane review investigating the benefit of routine follow up with CA125 surveillance in asymptomatic women after priamry treatment found that this did not increase overall survival, but the authors caution that the trials predated PARP inhibitor maintenance therapy and the increased use of secondary cytoreductive surgery.
See for treatment recommendations. Surgery is used for diagnosis, staging, and treatment.A
Stage II to IV ovarian cancer is treated with combination chemotherapy, generally carboplatin, paclitaxel, and a monoclonal antibody like bevacizumab or nariparib.A
Stages II through IV ovarian cancers are ovarian cancers are usually treated with combination chemotherapy (eg, intravenous carboplatin and paclitaxel) for 6 cycles.

Surgery is used for diagnosis, staging, and treatment. See . A systematic review found no RCTs but 11 retrospective observational studies support cytoreductive primary surgery with a goal of less than 1 cm residual disease. A second Cochrane review comparing cytoreductive surgery plus chemotherapy with chemotherapy alone found no relevant RCTs.
Surgery involves oophorectomy, partial omentectomy, and removal of visible cancer in the perineum or adjacent areas.

A systematic review of observational studies and clinical trials found no difference between minimally invasive staging and open staging for the outcome of death or recurrence (HR 0.92; 95% CI, 0.61-1.38) or all-cause mortality (HR 0.96; 95% CI, 0.49-1.89). However, the authors correctly caution that most of the studies were observational, at high risk of bias, and that most studies did not adjust for confounding.
A systematic review and consensus statement concluded that intraoperative fluorescence imaging using indocyanine green is a reliable method for lymphatic mapping.
A phase III RCT in 485 patients found that a second surgical cytoreduction was associated with morbidity and does not increase survival compared to proceeding directly to systemic therapy.

However, a second trial found that in women with a first relapse of ovarian cancer after a platinum free interval of at least 6 months had longer overall survival with the addition of cytoreductive surgery to chemotherapy (54 vs 46 month, p = 0.02).
A Cochrane review attempted to address whether laparoscopic surgery might be as effective as laparotomy, but there were no RCT trials to review.
Small bowel resection followed by re-anastomosis is the treatment of choice for small bowel obstruction.
Rectosigmoid obstruction is treated with transverse loop coostomy.
An updated Cochrane review of 43 trials and 4265 patients continues to show lack of clear evidence for role of surgery in malignant bowel obstruction.

A Cochrane review of corticosteroids for malignant bowel obstruction in women with advanced gynecological cancers found a non-significant trend toward a greater likelihood of the resolution of obstruction in women given corticosteroids, based on one small trial with 89 patients.
Anorexia is managed with megestrol acetate or steroids. Anemia is treated with transfusion and/or erythropoietin.
Early ovarian cancer requiring adjuvant chemotherapy (ie, stage IC epithelial ovarian cancer) should be treated with carboplatin.

Platinum-based chemotherapy (OR 0.93; 95% CI, 0.83-1.05) has a better hazard ratio for survival than nonplatinum-based combinations (OR 0.88; 95% CI, 0.79-0.98) and should be included in chemotherapy regimens for ovarian cancer.

The standard scheduling of platinum/taxol chemotherapy is every three weeks. A Japanese study suggested a benefit from dose-dense chemotherapy using weekly treatment, but a European trial of 1566 patients (ICON8) failed to show improvement in progression free survival with a weekly schedule compared to every three weeks and the dose-dense schedule was more toxic.

Consider conservative surgery (eg, laparoscopic unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and surgical staging) for young women with early-stage tumors (stages IA-IC) to preserve fertility. Management with conservative surgery assumes that the contralateral ovary is negative for tumor on biopsy and evaluation.

A Cochrane review found limited, low-quality evidence comparing ultraradical, extensive surgery with standard surgery for advanced epithelial ovarian cancer. There was a suggestion of better survival with extensive surgery.

A randomised trial of 647 patients compared lymphadenectomy with standard debulking surgery and found no improvement in progression-free or overall survival with lymphadenectomy, but there was an increased complication rate with the more extensive surgery.

For women with advanced ovarian epithelial cancer, a well designed randomized trial with 714 women found no difference between chemotherapy before cytoreductive surgery or maximal cytoreductive surgery followed by chemotherapy. A further recent RCT of 552 patients confirmed the non-inferiority of primary chemotherapy compared to primary surgery in advanced disease.

A Cochrane review of 5 RCTs and 1774 patients found no difference in survival between neoadjuvant chemotheerapy followed by surgery and primary surgery followed by adjuvant chemotherapy. The evidence was rated as good quality. The one possible factor for consideration of treatment was that neoadjuvant chemotherapy appeared to reduce post-operative complications and the need for stoma.

Secondary surgical cytoreduction did not increase overall survival compared to chemotherapy alone at relapse in a randomized trial with 485 women with a trend toward higher mortality with surgery (HR 1.29; 95% CI, 0.97-1.72).

However, a systematic review identified 3 RCTs with 1250 patients with recurrent ovarian cancer and found significantly improved progression free survival in women with secondary cytoreductive surgery followed by systemic therapy with systemic therapy alone (HR 0.70, 95% CI, 0.61-0.78) but no effect on overall survival (HR 0.93; 95% CI, 0.78- 1.10).

Studies suggest that intraperitoneal chemotherapy improves survival in patients with advanced ovarian cancer. However, this is not first-line therapy. Intraperitoneal therapy is associated with poorer quality of life than intravenous therapy.
Intraperitoneal chemotherapy shows a more favorable treatment outcome, but less favorable quality of life than intraperitoneal plus intravenous chemotherapy.

Hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC) added to cytoreductive surgery showed recurrence free and overall survival benefit in an RCT in a study of 255 women with Stage 3 ovarian cancer who had already been treated with at least 3 cycles of carboplatin and paclitaxel. Median recurrence free survival increased by approximately 4 months, and at 5 years mortality was lower (50% vs 62%, NNT = 8).

A systematic review and meta-anlysis of HIPEC suggests that a possible recurrence free and overall survival benefit may be limited to those patients with the residual tumors <1 cm at time of treatment.

Bevacizumab (a monoclonal antibody used in the treatment of cancer to stop the growth of new blood vessels) shows promise for recurrent ovarian tumors when administered with chemotherapy. But patients taking bevacizumab have a higher risk of gastrointestinal complications, thromboembolic disease, and hypertension. A Cochrane review of 2011 found preliminary evidence to support use of bevacizumab based on a meta-analysis of early results from two trials, with a reduction in the likelihood of disease progression in women with advanced ovarian cancer.

An updated Cochrane review of the action of angiogenesis inhibitors (bevacizumab and also tyrosine kinase inhibitors which block receptors with similar effect to bevacizumab) benefitted from inclusion of 50 RCTs, 13 in newly diagnosed patients and 37 in context of relapsed disease, with a total of over 14,000 patients. They found that bevacizumab appeared to provide increased progression free and overall survival in the platinum resistant relapsed groups, with some possible benefit in progression free survival for the platinum sensistive relapse group. However there was less evidence for benefit and more toxicity in the early stage group.
The epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitor pertuzumab when added to gemcitabine did not improve survival in a study with 131 women, although there was a strong trend (HR 0.66; 95% CI, 0.43-1.03).

In 2021 American Society of Clinical Oncology performed a systematic review of 17 randomized trials and produced a guideline. They recommend: Stage III/IV in complete or partial response to platinum based chemotherapy with high-grade serous or endometrial ovarian cancer: recommend maintenance therapy with niraparib Germline or somatic pathogenic variants in BRCA1 (g/sBRCA1) or BRCA2 (g/sBRCA2): treat with olaparib. Stage III-IV EOC with g/sBRCA1/2 and/or genomic instability and a partial or complete response to chemotherapy plus bevacizumab combination: consider adding olaparib to bevacizumab. Ovarian cancer who have not received a PARPi and have responded to platinum-based therapy regardless of BRCA mutation status: offer maintenance therapy (second line or more) with single-agent PARP inhibitor. Recurrent ovarian cancer that hasn't recurred within 6 months of platinum-based therapy, who have not received a PARPi and have a g/sBRCA1/2, or whose tumor demonstrates genomic instability: offer a PARP inhibitor.

A Cochrane systematic review with 599 patients suggests an increased progression free survival for women with recurrent platinum sensitive disease using the recently developed PARP inhibitors such as niraparib. Two recently published large RCTs confirm this progression free survival benefit. In one, the improvement in PFS was 16 months in the gBRCA cohort and 9 months in the non-gBRCA group.This was confirmed in a RCT of 733 patients with newly diagnosed advanced ovarian cancer who had a response to platinum based therapy, with a trend toward improved overall survival.

An updated Cochrane review including 15 RCTs and assessing impact of PARP inhibitors both in primary treatment of newly diagnosed ovarian cancer and in the setting of recurrent disease confirmed the lack of overall survival benefit from addition of PARP inhibitors to chemotherapy or compared against chemotherapy. There was as noted above a possible increase in progression free survival using PARP inhibitors as maintenance therapy but this was noted to be associated with significantly increased toxicity.

A trial randomized 1140 women with Stage III or IV high grade ovarian carcinoma to standard induction chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel with or without the addition of veliparib, followed by veliparib maintenance therapy. Progression free survival was longer in the veliparib group (35 vs 22 months, p < 0.001).
Adding olaparib to bevacizumab as maintenance therapy improved PFS somewhat (22 vs 17 months) in women with advanced cancer regardless of their BRCA mutation status.
Continuing treatment beyond primary chemotherapy using maintenance agents has been shown to improve progression free survival with both PARP inhibitor and VEGFR inhibitor in recent RCTs.

A trial randomized 453 women with platinum-resistant high-grade serous ovarian cancer to mirvetuximab soravtansine-gynx (MIRV, an antibody-drug conjugate that targets folate receptor alpha (FRa) or to chemotherapy with either paclitaxel, pegylated liposomal doxorubicin, or topotecan. Overall survival was longer with MIRV (16.5 vs 12.7 months, p =0.005).

A Cochrane review investigating the benefit of routine follow up with CA125 surveillance in asymptomatic women after priamry treatment found that this did not increase overall survival, but the authors caution that the trials predated PARP inhibitor maintenance therapy and the increased use of secondary cytoreductive surgery.
See for a summary of 5 year survival by stage and type of tumor from SEER cancer registry data.

feature.caption: Staging System for Ovarian Cancer.
feature.feature_body:
Staging Ovarian Cancer (FIGO System)*
I Confined to ovary
IA Confined to 1 ovary + ovarian capsule and surface intact + abdominal washings negative
IB Confined to 2 ovaries + Ovarian capsule and surface intact + abdominal washings negative
IC Present in 1 or both ovaries
IC1 Surgical spill
IC2 Capsule rupture before surgery or tumnor on ovarian surface
IC3 Malignant cells in the ascites or peritoneal washings
II One or both ovaries + other organs involved
IIA Cancer extended to uterus and/or tubes + abdominal washings negative
IIB Ovarian cancer extends to pelvic organs + abdominal washings negative
IIC Involves pelvic organs with cancer on outer surface of at least 1 ovary, ruptured capsule of cystic tumor and/or abdominal washings positive
III Involves 1 or both ovaries with cells beyond the pelvis to lining of the abdomen and/or lymph node involvement
IIIA Positive retroperitoneal lymph nodes and/or micrscopic metastasis beyond the pelvis
IIIA1 (i) Retroperitonel lymph nodes only <10 mm metastasis (ii) retroperitonela lymph nodes >10 mm
IIIA2 Micrscopic, extrapelvic peritoneal involvement (above the brim) ± retroperitoneal lymph nodes
IIIB Cancer in 1 or both ovaries with cancer noted by surgeon in abdomen but <2 cm across ± positive retroperitoneal lymph nodes. Includes extension to capsule of liver/spleen
IIIC Cancer in 1 or both ovaries with lymph node involvement and/or >2 cm across ± retroperitoneal lymph nodes. Includes extension to liver/spleen
IVA Plueral effusion with postitive cytology
IVB Hepatic and/or splenic parenchymal metastasis extending to extra abdominal organs
*Nodal location and metastasis are based on TNM system. FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) also recommends histologic classification and grading of epithelial cancer lesions. From Prat, Jaime. FIGO Guidelines Staging classification for cancer of the ovary, fallopian tube, and peritoneum. Int J Gynecol Obstet 2014;124:1–5.

feature.caption: Management of Ovarian Cancer by Stage and Tumor Type from the National Comprehensive Cancer Network.
feature.feature_body:
Stage of Tumor Tumor Type Treatment
Confined to ovary (stage 1) Dysgerminoma Conservative surgery*
Stage II-IV Dysgerminoma Surgery and chemotherapy (etoposide + cisplatin ± bleomycin)
Confined to ovary Immature teratoma Surgery
Stage I (grade 2 or grade 3), II-IV Immature teratoma Surgery + chemotherapy
Spread beyond ovary Mature teratoma Surgery + chemotherapy
Germ cell tumors Surgery + combination chemotherapy (bleomycin, etoposide, cisplatin)
Stages IA and IB Epithelial cell cancer TAH, salpingectomy and/or BSO, partial omentectomy (as needed) and peritoneal washings. For women desiring fertility, perform conservative surgery and avoid biopsy of normal contralateral ovary
Stage IC (consider for IB) Epithelial cell cancer Surgery and adjuvant chemotherapy
Stages IIA, IIB, and IIC Epithelial cell cancer Surgery, combination chemotherapy, and radiation
Stages III and IV Epithelial cell cancer Surgery, cytoreduction, removal of cancer from other organs and bulky nodes, and combination chemotherapy. l Cochrane 1418 (Level A)
Posttreatment follow-up of epithelial cell cancer
Every 2-4 months for 2 years, then 6 months for 3 years, then annually. Each visit: H&P, CA-125 on regular basis. Annual Pap and mammogram for patients with strong family history or older than 40 years
*Conservative surgery implies laparoscopic salpingo-oophorectomy and staging or the sparing of ovarian tissue in 1 or more ovaries and/or the uterus in anticipation of sparing fertility. Traditional surgery includes laparotomy with the removal of ovaries including aggressive cytoreductive surgery, when applicable.TAH denotes total abdominal hysterectomy; BSO, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy; H&P, history and physical.
